economics.title: Marketing Definition of a Product
economics.context: Review the marketing definition of a product as every good and service that can be exchanged to fulfil customer wishes and needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: In marketing terminology, a product refers only to physical goods and excludes services from the definition.
In marketing terminology, a product is every good and/or service that can be exchanged in order to fulfil the wishes and needs of customers.
Producer products are defined by whether an item is manufactured in a factory rather than by the customer who purchases it.
Consumer products are defined by retail packaging size rather than by whether the buyer is a household or business.
A printer is always a consumer product because households are the most visible end users of printers.
tactical_explanations:
Marketing treats a product as anything that can be exchanged to meet customer wishes and needs, including services. Limiting the term to physical goods alone drops maintenance contracts, consulting, and support out of the definition without reason.

So the statement is False.

Under the marketing definition, a product is every good and/or service that can be exchanged to fulfil customer wishes and needs. Tangible merchandise and intangible service work sit under the same label once an exchange is on the table.

So the statement is True.

Producer versus consumer labels turn on who buys, not on whether the item left a factory. A finished printer sold to another firm is still a producer product even though it is fully assembled merchandise. Factory origin, assembly line history, and industrial design do not decide the category. Marketing asks whether the purchaser is a business or a household in that exchange. Treating manufacture as the test misplaces the buyer criterion and would misclassify countless finished B2B goods.

So the statement is False.

Consumer-product status tracks whether the buyer is a private household, not how large the retail pack is. A bulky home appliance bought for domestic use remains a consumer product; a tiny office staple bought by a firm remains a producer product. Packaging size is not the classifying rule.

So the statement is False.

Printers sold into offices for commercial work are producer products even though households also buy printers. Visibility of home users does not freeze every printer into the consumer category. Classification follows the actual purchaser in each exchange, so "always consumer" is too absolute.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Alpine Sensors AG as a Separate Legal Person
economics.context: Three engineers incorporate Alpine Sensors AG in Austria so the firm itself can hold patents, hire staff, and face suppliers in its own name. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Once incorporated, Alpine Sensors AG is a legal entity of its own with rights and obligations comparable to those of natural persons in business life.
As a legal person, Alpine Sensors AG can own laboratory equipment and land, hire technicians, and close supply contracts in the company’s name.
If a supplier sues over unpaid circuit boards, the lawsuit is brought against Alpine Sensors AG rather than automatically against each engineer’s private name.
The founding engineers must personally manage every production shift because shareholders of a corporation are always also its day-to-day managers.
A hired plant manager at Alpine Sensors AG may run operations without owning any shares in the company.
tactical_explanations:
Incorporation gives Alpine Sensors AG its own legal personality. The company holds rights and duties in business life much as a natural person would when owning assets, hiring, or contracting, separate from the three engineers as private individuals.

So the statement is True.

As a legal person, Alpine Sensors AG can own lab gear and land, employ technicians, and sign supply contracts in the company name. Those acts attach to the firm, not to each founder’s private identity.

So the statement is True.

Supplier suits over unpaid boards are filed against Alpine Sensors AG as the contracting party. Creditors pursue the corporate defendant first rather than automatically naming every engineer’s private identity as the debtor on the face of the claim.

So the statement is True.

Shareholders fund and own the corporation; they are not forced to run every production shift. Alpine Sensors AG can hire managers and operators while founders remain owners without day-to-day shop-floor duty. Equating ownership with mandatory personal management confuses equity stakes with employment roles. Many corporations deliberately separate investors from operators so specialists run production. The engineers may choose to work in the plant, but corporate form does not compel that identity of owner and manager for every shift.

So the statement is False.

A hired plant manager can direct operations with zero shareholding. Management authority comes from appointment and employment, not from an automatic equity ticket, which is why ownership and operational control can diverge inside Alpine Sensors AG.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Impulse Buying Under Promotion
economics.context: Analyze how high-quality durable goods can be circulated among users instead of being discarded after brief use. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses bear no responsibility for consumer budgets when advertising encourages additional unplanned purchases.
Swapping quality garments at community events extends wear without each participant buying new low-cost items.
Refurbishment always wastes more resources than manufacturing a new unit regardless of product condition.

For electronics retailers in consumer electronics markets, businesses may create wishes and needs by continuously developing new products and advertising them, not only by responding to existing customer demand.
Event clothing must be purchased because rental services cannot supply outfits of higher quality than cheap retail goods.
tactical_explanations:
When ads push unplanned extras, firms help shape the spend that follows. Claiming zero responsibility for those budget overruns ignores how promotion works. Marketing that sparks impulse buys is not a neutral bystander.

So the statement is False.

Community swap events move quality garments between wearers without a trip to buy new low-cost replacements. Each swap extends fabric life and cuts demand for fresh cheap stock. Circulation replaces disposal-and-repurchase for that wardrobe slot.

So the statement is True.

Refurbishing a sound chassis with new batteries or screens often uses far less material than building a unit from raw inputs. Condition matters: a lightly used device is a candidate for refurbishment, not automatic scrap. Blanket claims that refurbishment always wastes more than new manufacture ignore those savings. Manufacturers and repair shops routinely choose remanufacture when the base product is still solid. The absolute wording is therefore false.

So the statement is False.

Electronics retailers refresh models and advertise features that shoppers had not requested. Creating new wishes sits alongside meeting stated demand. Continuous development plus promotion can manufacture desire, not only respond to it.

So the statement is True.

Premium rental racks often stock higher-quality eventwear than bargain retail racks. Clients need not purchase to access that tier. Saying rental cannot beat cheap retail quality invents a false limit.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Barter limits
economics.context: Two farmers swap eggs for vegetables without using money. Evaluate barter and money:. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Inflation refers to one shop's single price hike only, never to the general price level.
Division of labour across countries is impossible because climate never differs.
Because no euros change hands, this egg-for-vegetable swap involves no economic exchange at all.
Without money, storing value from perishable eggs into future purchases is harder than holding currency.
Barter economies never face problems comparing relative values of unlike goods.
tactical_explanations:
Inflation is a general price-level rise, not a single shop's isolated hike. One sticker change is not inflation by itself. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is False.

Climate and other differences across countries are exactly why cross-border specialisation occurs. Division of labour across countries is common, not impossible.

So the statement is False.

An agreed egg-for-vegetable swap is exchange even with no euros. Barter is exchange without money, not the absence of economic exchange. That reading follows directly from the scarce means named in the statement, not from a different chapter topic.

So the statement is False.

Perishable eggs are a poor store of value compared with currency balances that can buy a wide future basket. Without money, turning today's egg surplus into deferred purchasing power is harder.

Farmers in the stem can trade once, but holding value across time is clumsier when the "savings" spoil. That conclusion stays inside this statement's own nouns and does not borrow a different definition from another letter.

So the statement is True.

Barter economies struggle to compare unlike goods without a common measure. Comparison problems are a standard barter friction, not something those economies never face.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Working Capital and Short-Term Credit
economics.context: Consider a construction firm covering payroll gaps with short-term bank loans while shareholders debate whether to inject equity instead of adding more debt. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A business with a high proportion of loan capital might have difficulties obtaining more credit.
High gearing means capital expenditure should be funded only through additional bank loans at any interest rate offered.
Lenders may extend credit to a highly geared business only if acceptable collateral can be offered.
Revenue expenditure must never use short-term trade credit when the balance sheet already lists any loan capital.
Administration costs of bond issues are ignored because only equity carries issuance expenses.
tactical_explanations:
A business with a high proportion of loan capital might have difficulties obtaining more credit. Lenders already see elevated repayment risk before the next facility is discussed.

So the statement is True.

High gearing argues against funding capital expenditure only through additional bank loans at any rate offered. Internal funds or investors can be safer than accepting every expensive debt offer on the table.

So the statement is False.

Lenders may extend credit to a highly geared business only if acceptable collateral can be offered. Security becomes a gate when unsecured appetite is already exhausted by existing loans. Higher interest alone may not suffice if the lender wants assets pledged against further exposure. The construction firm's equity debate sits beside that collateral reality when debt is already heavy.

So the statement is True.

Revenue expenditure may still use short-term trade credit even when some loan capital already appears on the balance sheet. A blanket ban on supplier credit whenever any loan exists overstates gearing caution.

So the statement is False.

Bond issues also carry administration and flotation expenses, not only equity issues. Ignoring bond issuance costs because 'only equity has fees' misreads the cost comparison.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: PhoneFix screen repairs
economics.context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Replacing a cracked screen is labour performed for the customer, a service. A phone case sold at the counter is a tangible good. PhoneFix can offer both in one visit.

So the statement is True.

Spare parts arrive in limited monthly batches. Being a business does not create unlimited stock. When the batch runs down, further repairs wait. Scarcity of parts is exactly why the shop must prioritise jobs.

So the statement is False.

A decorative case bought for design rather than protection serves appearance and preference. That is a want, not a basic need for well-being. Functionally necessary repairs differ from optional styling accessories.

So the statement is True.

A working phone often supports work, school contact, and safety. Repairing it can restore a practical need, not merely a luxury whim. Excluding phones from economic analysis is artificial.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly parts batch cannot cover every cracked screen that walks in. PhoneFix must decide which jobs to accept, which to delay, and how to stretch inventory. That prioritisation is economising under scarcity. Unlimited-parts thinking would remove the need to choose; limited batches force ranking. The statement links the shop's constraint to careful allocation correctly.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: EU micro staff ceiling
economics.context: Consider a workshop that employs nine people with €1.8m turnover. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because staff are below ten, a firm remains a micro enterprise despite turnover above €2m.
Forty-five staff alone guarantees small classification even if turnover exceeds €10m.
Meeting the staff ceiling alone is sufficient for micro status regardless of turnover or balance sheet totals.
Under the EU definition, a micro enterprise may employ fewer than ten people.
A firm qualifies as micro because its balance sheet is below €2m, regardless of turnover above €2m.
tactical_explanations:
Headcount under ten is only one micro test. Turnover above €2m can still block micro status even with a tiny payroll. Staff alone never completes the EU micro definition.

So the statement is False.

Forty-five staff sit inside the small employee band, yet turnover above €10m can push the firm out of small status. Headcount guarantees nothing once the financial caps are breached.

So the statement is False.

Micro status needs fewer than ten people plus a financial test: turnover or balance sheet not above €2m. Meeting the staff ceiling while blowing past both financial caps fails the definition.

A nine-person firm with €3m turnover and a €3m balance sheet is not micro under those figures. Staff sufficiency alone is therefore not enough for the label.

So the statement is False.

Under the EU definition, a micro enterprise may employ fewer than ten people as its staff ceiling. That headcount limit is the employment half of the micro tests.

So the statement is True.

A balance sheet below €2m helps only if the other micro tests also hold. Turnover above €2m can still disqualify micro status even when the balance sheet looks small.

So the statement is False.

english.passage:
(1) When public debt stocks rise faster than nominal GDP for several consecutive years, markets begin to price not only solvency risk but also the political temptation to lean on the monetary authority. Fiscal dominance denotes a regime in which the path of primary balances is treated as given, so that the central bank must ultimately accommodate debt servicing through lower real rates, financial repression, or outright purchases of government paper. The textbook opposite—monetary dominance—keeps the inflation objective first and forces the fiscal authority to adjust taxes or spending. Between those poles sits a grey zone that advanced economies occupied after the global financial crisis and again during the pandemic: large exceptional bond purchases framed as liquidity support, accompanied by repeated assurances that the purchases were temporary, sterilised in spirit if not always on the balance sheet, and unrelated to financing the Treasury.

(2) Independence statutes were written precisely to raise the political cost of that accommodation. Operational independence typically covers instrument choice—policy rates, reserve requirements, the composition of the open-market book—while goal independence concerns the mandate itself. Even where statutes look strong on paper, credibility is an equilibrium outcome. Bond markets that believe a future government will rewrite the mandate, stack the board, or compel direct financing will demand higher term premia today. Conversely, a central bank that has spent years under-delivering on inflation may find that markets discount its promises even when the legal text is unchanged. Independence is therefore not a binary switch; it is a reputational asset that depreciates when policy repeatedly subordinates the inflation target to debt-service comfort.

(3) Debt monetisation is often caricatured as the printing press funding a single extravagant budget. In modern practice it is usually quieter. A central bank can expand its balance sheet by purchasing secondary-market government bonds, credit the sellers' reserve accounts, and leave the Treasury free to place new primary issuance into a market that has just absorbed a large buyer. If the bank later rolls those holdings indefinitely, the consolidated public sector has permanently replaced interest-bearing debt held by the private sector with non-interest-bearing (or low-interest) reserves. Whether that sequence is labelled quantitative easing, monetary financing, or "liquidity management" depends less on the accounting labels than on whether the purchases are expected to be reversed and whether fiscal policy adjusts when inflation threatens. Economists disagree on thresholds, but few deny that open-ended secondary-market support can functionally mimic primary monetisation when markets treat the central bank as the residual buyer.

(4) Critics of large-scale asset purchases emphasise distributional and financial-stability side effects: compressed term premia can fuel leverage in shadow banking, inflate asset prices unevenly, and blunt the signal that long rates normally send about scarcity of capital. Defenders reply that in a liquidity trap, with policy rates near the effective lower bound, such purchases were the least-bad way to prevent a collapse in aggregate demand and a self-fulfilling debt spiral. The empirical literature remains contested because identification is hard: crises that trigger QE also move fiscal balances, risk premia, and inflation expectations at the same time. What is less contested is the political economy lesson. Once a central bank has demonstrated that it can absorb large volumes of sovereign paper without an immediate inflation spike, the fiscal authority faces a weaker constraint on primary deficits—until inflation returns and the same institution must tighten into a stock of debt that has grown under its own earlier support.

(5) For applicants sitting a business-economics entrance exam, the practical takeaway is not to memorise slogans but to track the assignment of residual adjustment. Ask who is forced to move when debt dynamics look unsustainable: the finance ministry through primary surplus, or the monetary authority through accommodation. Ask whether secondary-market purchases are time-limited and paired with a credible exit, or whether markets price them as a standing put. And notice that "independence" without a hard budget constraint elsewhere in the polity is always provisional. Statutes raise the cost of capture; they do not abolish the incentive to capture when the alternative is politically costly consolidation.
english.passageTitle: Fiscal Dominance, Central-Bank Independence, and the Quiet Mechanics of Debt Monetisation

tasks.title: Task 1 — Regime definitions
tasks.context: Based on paragraphs (1)–(2), decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Fiscal dominance, as defined in the passage, treats the path of primary balances as given and requires the central bank to accommodate debt servicing.
Monetary dominance, in the passage's framing, keeps the inflation objective first and forces fiscal adjustment through taxes or spending.
The passage claims that post-crisis and pandemic bond purchases sat in a pure monetary-dominance regime with no grey-zone ambiguity.
Operational independence in the passage covers instrument choice such as policy rates and the open-market book, while goal independence concerns the mandate itself.
The passage treats central-bank independence as a binary legal switch that markets ignore once statutes are written.
tactical_explanations:
Paragraph (1) defines fiscal dominance as a regime in which primary balances are treated as given, so the central bank must ultimately accommodate debt servicing through lower real rates, financial repression, or purchases of government paper.

So the statement is True.

The same paragraph sets monetary dominance as the opposite pole: inflation objective first, with the fiscal authority forced to adjust taxes or spending.

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (1) places advanced economies after the global financial crisis and during the pandemic in a grey zone between the poles—large exceptional purchases framed as liquidity support—not in pure monetary dominance without ambiguity.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (2) distinguishes operational independence (instrument choice: rates, reserve requirements, open-market book composition) from goal independence (the mandate itself).

So the statement is True.

Paragraph (2) explicitly rejects the binary-switch view: independence is a reputational asset that depreciates when policy subordinates the inflation target, not a switch markets ignore once statutes exist.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Task 2 — Monetisation mechanics
tasks.context: Based on paragraph (3), decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The passage argues that modern debt monetisation is usually quieter than the caricature of a printing press funding one extravagant budget.
Secondary-market purchases that credit sellers' reserve accounts can leave the Treasury freer to place new primary issuance into a market that has just absorbed a large buyer.
If holdings are rolled indefinitely, the consolidated public sector permanently replaces private interest-bearing debt with reserves that are non-interest-bearing or low-interest.
The passage says accounting labels alone—QE versus monetary financing—are decisive regardless of exit expectations and fiscal adjustment.
Open-ended secondary-market support can functionally mimic primary monetisation when markets treat the central bank as the residual buyer.

tasks.title: Task 3 — Side effects and politics

So the statement is True.

So the statement is False.

Paragraph (4) states the political-economy lesson: demonstrated absorption without an immediate inflation spike weakens the fiscal primary-deficit constraint until inflation returns.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Task 8 — Grammar (conditionals / aspect)
tasks.context: Choose whether each sentence is grammatically and idiomatically correct English for a formal economics text.

tactical_explanations:
Inverted third-conditionals (Had … not …, … would have …) are correct formal English.

So the statement is True.

After if, use present/believe for a real conditional—not "would believe". Correct: If markets believe the purchases are temporary, …

So the statement is False.

The comparative correlative the more … the weaker … is standard and correct.

So the statement is True.

Negative inversion with Rarely has + subject + past participle is grammatical.

So the statement is True.

Neither … nor with two singular subjects takes a singular verb in careful formal usage here, but "is" with a plural-leaning reading of appointments is awkward; standard: Neither the statute nor the board appointments are irrelevant—or better, Neither X nor Y is irrelevant when both are singular. math.title: Union, Intersection, and Difference of Three Sets
statements: $A \setminus B = \{1, 2\}$.
$B \setminus A = A \setminus B$.
A and C are disjoint sets.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Unite $A$ and $B$:

$$A=\{1,2,3,4\}$$

$$B=\{3,4,5,6\}$$

$$1\in A\cup B$$

$$2\in A\cup B$$

$$3\in A\cup B$$

$$4\in A\cup B$$

$$5\in A\cup B$$

$$6\in A\cup B$$

$$A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Shared members:

$$3\in A$$

$$3\in B$$

$$4\in A$$

$$4\in B$$

$$1\in A$$

$$1\notin B$$

$$2\in A$$

$$2\notin B$$

$$A\cap B=\{3,4\}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Difference keeps members of $A$ that miss $B$:

$$1\in A$$

$$1\notin B$$

$$2\in A$$

$$2\notin B$$

$$3\in A$$

$$3\in B$$

$$4\in A$$

$$4\in B$$

$$A\setminus B=\{1,2\}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Compute the opposite difference:

$$5\in B$$

$$5\notin A$$

$$6\in B$$

$$6\notin A$$

$$B\setminus A=\{5,6\}$$

From letter C,

$$A\setminus B=\{1,2\}$$

$$\{5,6\}\neq\{1,2\}$$

so the two differences are unequal.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Disjointness needs empty intersection:

$$A=\{1,2,3,4\}$$

$$C=\{7,8,9\}$$

$$1\notin C$$

$$2\notin C$$

$$3\notin C$$

$$4\notin C$$

$$A\cap C=\emptyset$$

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
**Part 1: The sets.**

Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$, $B=\{3,4,5,6\}$, and $C=\{7,8,9\}$.

**Part 2: The operations.**

Intersection keeps shared members; union keeps anything that sits in at least one list, written once; difference $X\setminus Y$ keeps members of $X$ that miss $Y$. Two sets are disjoint when they share nothing. Scan $A$ against $B$: $3$ and $4$ sit in both, $1$ and $2$ miss $B$, and $5$ and $6$ miss $A$. Scan $A$ against $C$: no shared member.

math.title: Five separate age and consecutive-number stories
math.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A father is now four times as old as his son. In $20$ years the father will be twice as old as the son will be then. The son is now $10$ years old.
A mother is three times as old as her daughter. In $12$ years the mother will be twice as old as the daughter will be then. The daughter is now $12$ years old.
A father who is now $40$ will be $50$ in $20$ years.
If a father is now $40$ and his son is now $10$, their ages differ by $30$ years, and that gap does not change as both grow older.
Five years ago a father of $40$ and a son of $10$ were in the ratio five to one.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A present-age ratio together with a future-age ratio is one linear equation in the son's present age.

Let $s$ be the son's age now, in years. The father is now four times as old, so the father is now $4s$. In $20$ years the father will be twice as old as the son will be then:

$$4s + 20 = 2(s + 20)$$

$$4s + 20 = 2s + 40$$

$$2s = 20$$

$$s = 10$$

The son is now $10$ years old, and the father is now $40$. The claim is that same age $10$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A present-age ratio together with a future-age ratio is one linear equation in the daughter's present age.

Let $d$ be the daughter's age now, in years. The mother is now three times as old, so the mother is now $3d$. In $12$ years the mother will be twice as old as the daughter will be then:

$$3d + 12 = 2(d + 12)$$

$$3d + 12 = 2d + 24$$

$$d = 12$$

The daughter is now $12$ years old. The claim is that same age $12$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Ages grow by adding the elapsed time.

A father who is now $40$ will, after $20$ years, be

$$
40 + 20 =60
$$

He will be $60$, not $50$. The claimed $50$ would mean only $10$ years of growth from $40$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The difference of two ages is unchanged when both grow by the same number of years.

$$
40 - 10 = 30
$$

The gap is $30$ years now. After any common wait of $t$ years the ages are $40 + t$ and $10 + t$, and their difference is still $30$. The claim matches that constant gap.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Past ages are present ages minus the elapsed time, and a ratio is their quotient.

Five years ago the father was $35$ and the son was $5$:

$$
40 - 5 = 35
$$

$$
10 - 5 = 5
$$

$$
\frac{35}{5} = 7
$$

They were in the ratio seven to one, not five to one. Five to one would have required ages $35$ and $7$.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Five independent age claims. Translate a present ratio and a future ratio into one linear equation. Ages that grow together keep a constant gap.

math.solution_overview:
Solventis blends two drug suspensions, each with a fixed mg/mL concentration. Batch 1: 500 mL of A and 300 mL of B, 8,880 mg. Batch 2: 200 mL of A and 700 mL of B, 12,600 mg. A third batch's Suspension A volume was logged in liters, then converted to mL: 0.32 L $= 320$ mL of A, 450 mL of B, 9,700 mg recorded.

**Part 1: Building the system.**

Let $x$ = mg/mL concentration of Suspension A, $y$ = mg/mL concentration of Suspension B.

**1. Translate: Batch 1.** That observation becomes:

$$500x + 300y = 8880 \tag{1}$$

**2. Translate: Batch 2.** That observation becomes:

$$200x + 700y = 12600 \tag{2}$$

**Part 2: Solve.**

**1.** Divide Batch 1 by 100 and Batch 2 by 100:

$$
5x + 3y = 88.8, \qquad 2x + 7y = 126
$$

**2.** Multiply the first by 7 and the second by 3 so the $y$ coefficients both become $21y$:

$$
35x + 21y = 621.6, \qquad 6x + 21y = 378
$$

**3.** Subtract:

$$
(35x + 21y) - (6x + 21y) = 621.6 - 378
$$

$$
29x = 243.6 \Rightarrow x =  rac{243.6}{29} = 8.4
$$

**4.** Substitute $x = 8.4$ into $2x + 7y = 126$:

$$
2(8.4) + 7y = 126 \Rightarrow 16.8 + 7y = 126 \Rightarrow 7y = 109.2 \Rightarrow y = 15.6
$$

**5.** Audit Batch 3 ($0.32$ L $= 320$ mL of A):

$$
320(8.4) + 450(15.6) = 2688 + 7020
$$

$$
= 9708
$$

versus 9,700 mg recorded, an 8 mg discrepancy.

**Answer.** Suspension A = 8.4 mg/mL | Suspension B = 15.6 mg/mL | Batch 3 predicted = 9,708 mg (vs. 9,700 mg recorded).

math.title: Double Composition and Leading Match
math.context: A line and a parabola are given by $f(x)=4x+2$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{1}{16}$, $B=-\frac{1}{2}$, $C=-\frac{5}{4}$.
Because $f-g$ can be mistaken for a cubic, the graphs may meet three times.
At the axis of $g$, the gap $f-g$ equals $\frac{17}{4}$.
Completing the square gives $g(x)=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ is a three-coefficient linear system. The $x^{2}$ coefficients force $A$ first, because only $Af^{2}$ produces $x^{2}$.

$$1=A\cdot 16$$

$$A=\frac{1}{16}$$

Equating the $x$ coefficients then gives $B$, and the constant terms give $C$.

$$B=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$C=-\frac{5}{4}$$

Substituting the three numbers back reproduces $g$ identically.

Substituting the three numbers back reproduces $g$ identically: $A\cdot 16=1$ recovers the leading coefficient.

$$A=\frac{1}{16}$$

Matching forces the claimed triple.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The difference $f-g$ is quadratic, not cubic: $f$ has no $x^{2}$ term that could combine with $g$ to raise the degree.

$$f(x)-g(x)=-x^{2}+5x+4$$

A quadratic equation has at most two real roots, so three meetings are impossible. The discriminant $25+16=41>0$ gives exactly two meetings. A quadratic cannot hide a third root.

$$f-g=-x^{2}+5x+4$$

The graphs meet twice, not three times.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The two orders of nesting are different maps. Evaluate both at the origin.

$$f(0)=2$$

$$g(2)=4-2-2$$

$$g(2)=4-2$$

$$g(2)=2$$

$$g(2)=2-2$$

$$g(2)=0$$

$$g(0)=-2$$

$$f(-2)=-8+2$$

$$f(-2)=-6$$

$$f(-2)=0\neq -6$$

Evaluate both nested orders at the origin and compare.

$$g(f(0))=0$$

$$f(g(0))=-6$$

Composition does not commute for this pair.

The two orders of nesting are different maps; a single input $x=0$ already separates them.

$$f(g(0))=0\neq -6$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The vertical gap at the axis is the difference of the two heights there. First locate the axis, then evaluate both models.

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=4\qquad g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{4}
$$

The gap is $4-(-9/4)=25/4$, not $17/4$.

$$
\frac{25}{4}\neq\frac{17}{4}
$$

The number $17/4$ would be $f(1/2)-1$, dropping the vertex depth. The gap at the axis is $\frac{25}{4}$, not $\frac{17}{4}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Completing the square isolates the axis shift from half the middle coefficient, then restores the constant so the rewritten formula matches the original polynomial.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-x-2$$

Halve the middle coefficient of the monic quadratic factor.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}$$

The axis shift is the opposite of that half-coefficient.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h=\frac{1}{2}$$

Evaluate the original rule at the axis to read the completed-square height.

$$g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{4}$$

Assemble the stretch, the shift, and the height.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-\frac{9}{4}$$

That matches the claimed completed-square form.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$$

So the statement is True.

math.title: Two Shuttle Fare Timers Under a Wait Cap
math.context: Two municipal shuttle apps quote wait time for a trip of distance $d>0$ kilometres. App L follows $L(d)=a d^{\frac{1}{2}}$ minutes and App Q follows $Q(d)=k d$ minutes, with both coefficients unpublished. A logged $25$ km trip on App L quoted $20$ minutes, and a logged $100$ km trip on App Q quoted $20$ minutes. A service-level agreement caps wait at $20$ minutes. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The two apps quote the same wait at two different positive distances.
Once App L quotes a shorter wait than App Q, App Q never catches up.
App L's wait per kilometre falls as the trip gets longer.
Under the $20$-minute cap, App L can serve trips longer than $30$ kilometres.
At $400$ kilometres both apps already quote more than $70$ minutes.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The two apps quote the same wait when

$$L(d)=Q(d)$$

. The overview recovered

$$L(d)=4d^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

 and

$$Q(d)=\frac{1}{5}d$$

, so

$$4d^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{5}d$$

$$d-20d^{\frac{1}{2}}=0$$

$$d^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigl(d^{\frac{1}{2}}-20\bigr)=0$$

The roots are

$$d=0$$

 and

$$d=400$$

. On $d>0$ they meet only once.

They do not quote the same wait at two different positive distances.

The computed figure disagrees with the claim.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

The overview recovered

$$L(d)=4d^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

 and

$$Q(d)=\frac{1}{5}d$$

Their ratio is

$$\frac{Q(d)}{L(d)}=\frac{1}{20}d^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

which is strictly increasing for $d>0$. Once the ratio passes $1$, it cannot return to $1$, so App Q cannot catch App L again.

After App L is shorter, App Q stays longer.

The computed figure agrees with the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Read the exponent from the overview before comparing growth rates.

App L's wait per kilometre is the recovered law divided by distance:

$$\frac{L(d)}{d}=4d^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$

The leftover exponent is negative, so that ratio falls as the trip gets longer.

Wait per kilometre on App L falls.

The computed figure agrees with the claim.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Start from the calibrated closed form in the overview.

Under the $20$-minute cap, App L can serve distances with $L(d)\le 20$. The overview recovered

$$L(d)=4d^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

, so

$$4d^{\frac{1}{2}}=20$$

$$d=25$$

The longest legal App L trip is $25$ km, which is not longer than $30$ km.

App L cannot serve trips longer than $30$ kilometres under the cap.

The computed figure disagrees with the claim.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The overview recovered

$$L(d)=4d^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

 and

$$Q(d)=\frac{1}{5}d$$

. At $400$ kilometres:

$$L(400)=4\cdot 20$$

$$L(400)=80$$

$$Q(400)=\frac{400}{5}$$

$$Q(400)=80$$

math.solution_overview:
App L quotes $L(d)=ad^{\frac{1}{2}}$ minutes and App Q quotes $Q(d)=kd$ minutes, for trip distance $d>0$ kilometres. A $25$ km trip on App L quoted $20$ minutes, and a $100$ km trip on App Q quoted $20$ minutes. Wait is capped at $20$ minutes.

**Part 1: Building the model.**

Let $d$ = trip distance in kilometres. Each log pins one coefficient, because each exponent is given.

math.title: Delivery Van: Cubic Speed Against a Short Table
math.context: A delivery van leaves the depot with modelled speed $$v(t)=0.0004t^{3}-0.036t^{2}+0.9t$$ in m/s. A second van is timed from the depot; its distances are in the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

The average speed of the second van over the $40$ s is $11$ m/s.
That whole-run average exceeds $45$ km/h.
The highest interval speed of the second van is on $[0,8]$.
The speed $v$ of the first van is a cubic polynomial in $t$.

**A.** → True

Speed is falling when the derivative of the modelled cubic is negative, so differentiate first.

$$v(t)=0.0004t^{3}-0.036t^{2}+0.9t$$

$$v'(t)=0.0012t^{2}-0.072t+0.9$$

At $t=40$ that quadratic equals

$$0.0012\cdot 1600-0.072\cdot 40+0.9$$

$$v'(t)=1.92-2.88+0.9$$

$$0.0012\cdot 1600-0.072\cdot 40+0.9$$

$$v'(t)=-0.06$$

.

$$v'(40)=-0.06$$

A negative value means the first van is slowing down.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Whole-run average speed is total distance over total time, read from the last column of the table.

$$s(40)=440$$

Divide by the $40$ s recorded from the depot:

$$\frac{440}{40}$$

$$s(40)=11$$

That quotient is $11$ m/s, matching the claimed whole-run average of the second van. The table starts at $0$ m, so no offset has to be subtracted.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$

$$

The converted average is $39.6$ km/h. The comparison asked for is the strict inequality

$$39.6>45$$

which fails. The second van's whole-run average stays below $45$ km/h, not above it, by about $5$ km/h.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Interval speeds are the successive distance jumps divided by the common $8$ s width.

$$6,\quad 10,\quad 14,\quad 14,\quad 11$$

Those five rates come from the jumps $48,80,112,112,88$. The largest value is $14$, attained on $[16,24]$ and on $[24,32]$, not on the opening block.

$$

$$v(t)=t(0.0004t^{2}-0.036t+0.9)$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

The speed model is therefore a cubic polynomial in $t$.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Graph comparison — force $k$ versus factor $1+r$
math.context: The figure sketches $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ against $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^{t}$ for one positive pair with $e^{k}\neq 1+r$. Interpret claims in letters $P_0>0$, $k$, $r>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $e^{k}>1+r>1$, then $P(t)>Q(t)$ for every $t>0$.
Both paths share the same initial value $P_0$.
The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path whenever $r=k>0$.
With fixed unequal multipliers, the two paths cannot touch at three distinct positive times.
Log-gap $\ln P(t)-\ln Q(t)$ equals $\bigl(k-\ln(1+r)\bigr)t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Under $e^{k}>1+r>1$ the continuous one-year factor strictly exceeds the discrete factor.

$$\frac{P(t)}{Q(t)} = \left(\frac{e^{k}}{1+r}\right)^{t}>1\qquad(t>0)$$

Hence $P(t)>Q(t)$ for every positive time.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Both formulas evaluate at time zero to the common initial level.

$$
P(0) = P_0 e^{0} = P_0
$$

$$
Q(0) = P_0(1+r)^{0} = P_0
$$

The paths share the same start.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

When $r=k>0$, compare one-year multipliers by the standard inequality.

$$e^{k}>1+k = 1+r$$

Raising to the power $t>0$ and multiplying by $P_0$ yields $P(t)>Q(t)$. The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Agreement at a positive time $t$ requires

$$e^{kt} = (1+r)^{t}$$

$$e^{k} = 1+r$$

whenever $t\neq 0$. If the multipliers are unequal, no positive $t$ works at all, so the paths certainly cannot touch at three distinct positive times.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Take logs of both paths and subtract.

$$
\ln P(t)-\ln Q(t) = kt-t\ln(1+r) = \bigl(k-\ln(1+r)\bigr)t
$$

That is exactly the claimed log-gap.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Compare continuous and discrete rivals through their ratio of one-year multipliers.

$$\frac{P(t)}{Q(t)}=\exp\bigl((k-\ln(1+r))t\bigr)$$

Shared start $P_0$, at most one later agreement unless the multipliers match, and for $r=k>0$ continuous leads because $e^{k}>1+k$.

math.title: Maintenance time per effective unit
math.context: A plant models total maintenance hours by $H(n)=2n^{2}+8n$ when it runs $n>0$ machines. Maintenance time per effective unit is $T(n)=\dfrac{H(n)}{n+1}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The derivative is $T'(n)=\dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}$.
$T'(n)>0$ for every $n>0$.
$T'(n)=\dfrac{2n+8}{n+1}$ after cancelling a common factor incorrectly.
There exists some $n>0$ for which $T'(n)=0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Maintenance time per effective unit is the quotient $T(n)=\dfrac{2n^{2}+8n}{n+1}$. Apply the quotient rule with numerator $u=2n^{2}+8n$ and denominator $v=n+1$:

$$
T(n) = \dfrac{2n^{2}+8n}{n+1}
$$

$$
u(n) = 2n^{2}+8n
$$

$$
v(n) = n+1
$$

$$
u'(n) = 4 n + 8
$$

$$
v'(n) = 1
$$

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{(4 n + 8)(n+1) - (2n^{2}+8n)(1)}{(n+1)^{2}}
$$

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{(4n+8)(n+1)-(2n^{2}+8n)\cdot 1}{(n+1)^{2}}
$$

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}
$$

which matches the claimed formula.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $n=1$ into that derivative:

$$
T'(1) = \dfrac{2+4+8}{2^{2}}
$$

$$
T'(1) = \dfrac{14}{4}
$$

$$
T'(1) = \dfrac{7}{2}
$$

Do not evaluate $T(1)=\dfrac{10}{2}=5$ when the claim asks for the slope. The computed derivative matches.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For $n>0$ the numerator $2n^{2}+4n+8=2(n^{2}+2n+4)$ is a sum of positive terms (discriminant $4-16<0$), and the denominator $(n+1)^{2}$ is positive. Hence

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}>0
$$

for every $n>0$. A positive derivative means $T$ is strictly increasing.

$$
2n^{2}+4n+8 = 2(n^{2}+2n+4)
$$

which matches the claim.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Cancelling factors incorrectly would produce $\dfrac{2n+8}{n+1}$, but the true derivative after the quotient rule is

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}
$$

Those expressions are not identical — the false one drops both the quadratic numerator structure and the squared denominator. The statement is False. Rephrasing the claim cannot repair an algebraic contradiction.

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{2n+8}{n+1}
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

For $n>0$ the numerator $2n^{2}+4n+8$ never vanishes (discriminant $4-16<0$) and the denominator stays positive, so

$$
T'(n) = \dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}>0
$$

throughout. A strictly positive derivative never hits zero, so no such root exists and

$$
T'(n) = 0
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Maintenance hours are $H(n)=2n^{2}+8n$, and time per effective unit is the quotient

$$T(n)=\dfrac{2n^{2}+8n}{n+1}$$

The quotient rule simplifies to the single fraction

$$T'(n)=\dfrac{2n^{2}+4n+8}{(n+1)^{2}}$$

At $n=1$ one finds $T'(1)=\dfrac{7}{2}$. The numerator $2n^{2}+4n+8=2(n^{2}+2n+4)$ has discriminant $4-16<0$, so it stays positive for every $n$; together with the positive denominator this forces $T'(n)>0$ for all $n>0$, and in particular $T'$ never vanishes. Cancelling factors incorrectly would produce the false expression $\dfrac{2n+8}{n+1}$.

math.title: Distributing Candies (Stars and Bars)
math.context: 10 identical pieces of candy are distributed at random among 4 distinct children, where each of the distributions counted by the stars-and-bars method is equally likely.
statements: The total number of distinct ways to distribute the 10 candies among the 4 children is 286.
The probability that a specific child receives no candy at all is greater than 23%.
The probability that a specific child receives at least 5 candies is less than 20%.
The probability that every one of the 4 children receives at least one candy is exactly 42/143.
The probability that a specific child receives no candy is more than double the probability that a specific child receives at least 5 candies.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This statement asks for the total number of distinct ways to distribute the $10$ candies among the $4$ children. This is a classic stars-and-bars problem, where we are looking for the number of non-negative integer solutions to the equation $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 10$. The formula for such a calculation, with $n$ identical items and $k$ distinct bins, is $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$.

For $n=10$ candies and $k=4$ children, we calculate:

$$
N_{\text{total}} = \binom{10+4-1}{4-1}
$$

$$
N_{\text{total}} = \binom{13}{3}
$$

$$
\binom{13}{3} = \dfrac{13!}{3!(13-3)!}
$$

$$
\dfrac{13!}{3!(10)!} = \dfrac{13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}
$$

$$
13 \cdot 12 = 156
$$

$$
156 \cdot 11 = 1716
$$

$$
\dfrac{1716}{6} = 286
$$

To determine the total number of distinct ways to distribute the candies, we use the stars-and-bars formula. For $n$ identical items distributed among $k$ distinct bins, the total number of ways is given by $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$. In this scenario, $n = 10$ candies and $k = 4$ children.

The total number of possible distributions, denoted $N_{\text{total}}$, is calculated as:
$$N_{\text{total}} = \binom{10+4-1}{4-1}$$
